The manybar goatfish, Parupeneus multifasciatus, is a benthic forager commonly found on coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded size of 31.5 centimeters [Li = 31.5 centimeters] in fork length, a value derived from photographs of captured individuals using a length-length conversion from total length. The wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae is estimated at 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], a mass calculated from the spherical volume of an egg with a diameter of approximately 1 millimeter. This minuscule initial size reflects the pelagic spawning strategy typical of the family Mullidae, where small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column. Larvae are lecithotrophic upon hatching, relying entirely on their yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The duration of this yolk-sac stage is temperature-dependent, but the species generally produces a large number of small offspring, which face high mortality rates during their early planktonic life.

Sexual maturation in Parupeneus multifasciatus occurs once individuals attain a fork length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. At this size, vitellogenesis and spermiation are initiated in females and males, respectively, marking the transition from a juvenile to a reproductively viable stage. Under the typical thermal conditions of tropical reef environments, approximately 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the maximum reproductive output of this species has been quantified through field observations. The total annual fecundity reaches approximately 26,432 eggs per year, which corresponds to roughly 26,432 eggs released in a single clutch per year [Ri = roughly 26,432 eggs released in a single clutch per year], with one spawning event each year [F_R_i = one spawning event each year]. This combination of an exceptionally high clutch size with an annual spawning frequency results in a substantial lifetime fecundity, a common life-history trait among small, iteroparous reef fishes that face high predation pressure.

The lifespan of the manybar goatfish has been studied through mark-recapture programs and otolith-based aging. In waters maintained at a mean temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the oldest documented individuals exhibit a maximum longevity of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], is relatively modest for a member of the Mullidae, a family that includes species living for more than a decade at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The comparatively short life expectancy is likely linked to the species' high metabolic rate and its elevated daily energy expenditure required for continuous foraging on benthic invertebrates. Juvenile fish recruit to seagrass beds and sandy flats where they grow rapidly, reaching the size necessary to join adult schools. Mortality during the first year of life is substantial, with only a small fraction of the cohort surviving to reproductive age.

A comparative analysis of growth patterns indicates that the ultimate fork length of 31.5 centimeters [Li = 31.5 centimeters] represents the asymptotic size these fish approach after several years of growth. This value was obtained by applying a conversion factor of 0.9 to a total length of 14 centimeters recorded in a photographic reference, demonstrating that adult body size remains relatively small. In contrast, the minimum size required for puberty at 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] is a developmental milestone reached relatively early in the species' life history, allowing individuals to begin contributing to the population before attaining full adult size. This early maturation is an adaptive response to high extrinsic mortality rates, ensuring that some offspring are produced even if an individual does not survive to reach the maximum size. The trade-off between somatic growth and reproductive investment is thus heavily skewed toward early reproduction.

The initial mass of the newly spawned egg, calculated as 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], provides a critical baseline for understanding the energetic constraints acting on early larval stages. At a stable environmental temperature of approximately 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the entire life cycle from egg to natural senescence in Parupeneus multifasciatus spans a maximum of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], highlighting the rapid pace of life in this tropical goatfish. Given the high annual reproductive output expressed through approximately 26,432 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 26,432 eggs per spawning event], a single female can release tens of thousands of eggs over her lifetime. This combination of a very small initial size, early maturity at a fork length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], and a short but prolific reproductive window is characteristic of an opportunistic life-history strategy, well suited to variable environmental conditions on patch reefs where competition for space and food is intense.
